steps.text:
"Algorist" is the term for digital artists who make algorithmic art. Among the pioneering algorists are Vera Molnár, Dóra Maurer and Gizella Rákóczy.

The algorists formally started corresponding and establishing their identity as artists after a panel at SIGGRAPH in 1995 that was called "Art and Algorithms". Jean-Pierre Hébert and Roman Verostko were the co-founders. Hébert is credited with coining the term, and also with its definition, which he wrote in the form of his own algorithm:

if (creation && object of art && algorithm && one's own algorithm) {

return * an algorist *

} else {

return * not an algorist *

### Types

Artists can write code that makes complex and dynamic visual compositions.

Cellular automata can be used to generate artistic patterns that have an appearance of randomness. They can also be used to modify images such as photographs, by applying a transformation, for example the stepping stone rule (which gives an impressionist style), over and over until the artistic effect that is wanted is achieved. People have also explored using them in music.

- fractal art: computer-generated fractals, colouring chosen for attractive effect
  - especially in western world, not drawn/painted by hand
  - usually made indirectly with fractal-generating software; three phases: set parameters, run possibly lengthy calculation, evaluate product
  - sometimes other graphics programs modify images = post-processing
  - non-fractal imagery may be integrated
- genetic/evolutionary art: genetic algorithms develop images iteratively, selection each "generation" by artist's rule
- not only produced by computers -> Wendy Chun
  - [quote: Chun on software as metaphor for metaphor; Weizenbaum, "effective procedures"]
- Jack Ox (American artist): algorithms -> paintings visualizing music, no computer
  - visual performances of extant scores: Bruckner's Eighth Symphony, Kurt Schwitters' Ursonate
  - later with collaborator Dave Britton: 21st Century Virtual Color Organ, uses computer coding + algorithms
- ambigram generators auto-generating ambigrams since 1996

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
"Algorist" is the term for digital artists who make algorithmic art. Among the pioneering algorists are Vera Molnár, Dóra Maurer and Gizella Rákóczy.

The algorists formally started corresponding and establishing their identity as artists after a panel at SIGGRAPH in 1995 that was called "Art and Algorithms". Jean-Pierre Hébert and Roman Verostko were the co-founders. Hébert is credited with coining the term, and also with its definition, which he wrote in the form of his own algorithm:

if (creation && object of art && algorithm && one's own algorithm) {

return * an algorist *

} else {

return * not an algorist *

### Types

Artists can write code that makes complex and dynamic visual compositions.

Cellular automata can be used to generate artistic patterns that have an appearance of randomness. They can also be used to modify images such as photographs, by applying a transformation, for example the stepping stone rule (which gives an impressionist style), over and over until the artistic effect that is wanted is achieved. People have also explored using them in music.

Fractal art is made up of different kinds of computer-generated fractals, where the colouring is chosen so that the effect is attractive. Especially in the western world, fractal art is not drawn or painted by hand. Usually it is created indirectly with the help of fractal-generating software, which goes through three phases: the parameters of suitable fractal software are set, then the possibly lengthy calculation is executed, and then the product is evaluated. Sometimes other graphics programs are used to modify the images that were produced even more. This is called post-processing. Non-fractal imagery can also be put into the artwork.

Genetic or evolutionary art uses genetic algorithms to develop images step by step, and at each "generation" a selection is made according to a rule that the artist defined.

But algorithmic art is not only made by computers. Wendy Chun explains:

> Software is unique in its status as metaphor for metaphor itself. As A universal imitator/machine, it encapsulates a logic of general substitutability; a logic of ordering and creative, animating disordering. Joseph Weizenbaum has argued that computers have become metaphors for "effective procedures," that is, for anything that can be solved in a prescribed number of steps, such as gene expression and clerical work.

Jack Ox, an American artist, has used algorithms to make paintings that visualize music, and she did it without using a computer. Two examples are visual performances of extant scores, Anton Bruckner's Eighth Symphony and Kurt Schwitters' Ursonate. Later she and her collaborator Dave Britton created the 21st Century Virtual Color Organ, which does use computer coding and algorithms.

There have been ambigram generators that generate ambigrams automatically since 1996.

### Types

Cellular automata can be used to generate artistic patterns with an appearance of randomness, or to modify images such as photographs by repeatedly applying a transformation such as the stepping stone rule (giving an impressionist style) until the desired artistic effect is achieved.[4] Their use has also been explored in music.[5]

Genetic or evolutionary art uses genetic algorithms to develop images iteratively, selecting at each "generation" according to a rule defined by the artist.[8,9]

Algorithmic art is not only produced by computers. As Wendy Chun explains:[10]

> Software is unique in its status as metaphor for metaphor itself. As A universal imitator/machine, it encapsulates a logic of general substitutability; a logic of ordering and creative, animating disordering. The American artist Jack Ox has used algorithms to produce paintings that visualize music without using a computer. Two examples are visual performances of extant scores, such as Anton Bruckner's Eighth Symphony[11,12] and Kurt Schwitters' Ursonate.[13,14] Later, she and her collaborator Dave Britton created the 21st Century Virtual Color Organ, which does use computer coding and algorithms.[15]
